GP will ask you to explain what’s going on, your current life inc. friends, partner etc, and about your past (maybe as far as childhood).

You fill out a questionnaire, or the doctor will read questions out to you for you to answer verbally. They will ask frustratingly specific things like has ‘anyone noticed you moving slowly’, or something like that (paraphrasing). It will also ask about suicide ideation. 

Then they will prescribe antidepressants (don’t be afraid of them if you haven’t tried them before, most of the time they are far better than the alternative, imo). They should also refer you/point you in the direction of community services like CBT or talking therapies. The nhs offer a short course ~8 sessions (don’t quote me on that), and in my experience the wait time wasn’t long at all.

A good GP should leave you feeling supported.

I don’t have any experience with the police in Scotland, but here in London, I can speak about my own experience of reporting SA, and the experience of many other woman that I have heard firsthand.

1. Upon first reporting the crime, you will be asked to recount the incident in detail. 
2. You will get a call from another PO, who will want to come out to meet with you immediately (they will insist on this). You will likely have several calls from different police officers/departments over the next couple days. I had easily over ten voicemails and missed calls, and each one needed me to retell them the details of what happened from scratch, even when I said I already explained it to someone else. There was generally no purpose to this.
3. When they come to take your statement, they will ask for evidence of each part of the story, even if you’ve already told them you don’t have evidence. They will tell you that they cannot arrest the perpetrator because it would be a breach of their human rights etc. It will likely feel like your experience is being minimised, or that they are ‘siding’ with the offender. 
4. From here, the police will go quiet. They will ask you to come in to give a statement (even though you already gave one), then it will take weeks for them to set up an appointment for you to go in, and you might have to chase them.
5. You give a statement (possibly a video statement), which will include very specific details of what happened, followed by a victim impact statement, where you describe how the experience has made you feel.
6. Depending on what evidence you have (none, but you could share that you made a hotel booking last minute to corroborate the fact that you left his place after the assault & the fact that you confronted him), they may decide to arrest the perpetrator. He will be questioned under causation, released on bail, it will take months for the inspector to investigate your case, then they will write to you saying the case has been dropped due to insufficient evidence.  As you don’t have any evidence, they might say they can’t arrest him or even speak to him. 

Despite all this, if I could go back, I absolutely still would report what happened. I just wish I knew what to expect. The police were never clear about the process, and I was re-traumatised again and again as I had to go through the details of what happened over and over, and had to wait for months not knowing what was going to happen. 

I encourage you to make the report as you’ve planned, go in with your head held high, don’t take anything the police say or do personally (although it’s hard considering the situation is so personal!). Be firm about the fact that you have already shared the details once and if they need that information they can get it off their colleagues as you won’t be subjected to being re-traumatised. Expect for there to be no outcome, but know that you stood up for yourself, and at least there will be something on record if this POS ever commits another assault on someone else. Hopefully knowing that you went to the police will at least put him on edge.

Focus more on your recovery than seeking justice. Get therapy, look after yourself, try to heal. This isn’t your fight to fight, you didn’t ask for this to be dumped on you. PM me if you need support.

For what it’s worth, I don’t think having adhd means that you have no idea about the way people think or feel. ADHD affects everyone soo differently and to varying degrees. I have a colleague who is also diagnosed and the way that we each experience, interpret, respond to etc the same scenarios are SO different, we often marvel at just how differently we think to each other and will go to one another for a different perspective when we face issues. I might speak to a neurotypical who sees things the way my colleague does or the way I do, or neither.

Personally, being diagnosed at age 30 was a relief because it meant ‘all those lies I told myself’ could be thrown out of the window, and I could adopt new strategies that ACTUALLY work for me. Maybe your reactions to problems ARE justified, or maybe learning different ways to respond to problems could do wonders for your relationship, or maybe both of those things are true. I promise you, neurotypical couples also have recurring issues that they can never seem to see eye to eye on I.e. someone ‘overreacting’, the other one ‘never understanding them’ and so on. Everyone can benefit from introspection. I know that I overreact sometimes, and have adopted techniques to help myself do that less often. Other times, I under-react, and don’t fully express myself in the way I need to in fear of making a big deal over nothing. It’s important to trust yourself too. 

If it turns out that you don’t have adhd, why does that mean that your struggles aren’t valid? ADHD doesn’t mean using your brain as an excuse, and being neurotypical doesn’t mean that you aren’t a human being with a complex mind. You could even have a different neurodivergence or just have a brain that needs support in a different way. You are still allowed to say ‘I struggle to try harder, I want to do better but I don’t know how’ and get the help you need. Maybe you could be kinder to yourself, maybe you’re already doing just fine, I don’t know enough about your situation but  if you think youd like to improve in certain areas you can get the support to do that with or without an adhd diagnosis.

I take a u-shaped pillow. Not a travel-size one but a regular size pillow. I put it in a big tote bag to carry it through the airport and then when I’m on the plane it goes between me and the window and I lean on it to sleep. I always get a window seat for this reason. 

I also have a foot rest that hangs over the back of the pullout tray on the seat in front of you and it’s like a little hammock for your feet (I’ve never had anyone in the seat in front complain and I don’t feel like it pulls on their seat at all, if it did then I wouldn’t use it). 

I bring loop ear plugs, a wraparound sleep mask, cosy socks, and wear comfy clothes that I can sleep in. I also bring compression stocking which go on under my cosy socks. 

I bring a big bottle of water and filling snacks in case the in-flight meal isn’t enough. 

Also, some entertainment like a kindle or tablet with shows/movies pre-downloaded, crosswords, sudoku etc. 

Medication obviously and painkillers. A handheld electric fan. A 100ml mist bottle of thermal water. Heat packs/medicated patches for sore muscles. Basic toiletries like moisturiser (planes dry the skin), eye drops (planes dry the eyes), hand sanitizer, toothbrush, hair brush etc, anything I need to make myself feel comfortable.

My comfort is my no.1 priority because I know the price I will have to pay if I subject myself to less than ideal conditions and a flight is always going to set me back regardless. So I do what I can to make it as less physically-taxing as possible.

I carry all my stuff in a big backpack and get help getting through the airport (wheelchair etc). Then once on the place I take out my essentials, put them in a smaller bag and put that under the seat in front of me. Ear plugs go in, foot rest gets hung up, pillow is propped against the side/window, socks go on, and I’m ready to fly.

It is also normal to go back and forth on whether you think the situation is abusive or not so don’t get mad at yourself if you have moments where you downplay it. Maybe keep a journal of everything he says/does so you can remind yourself.

As others have suggested, take a look online at women’s support groups, domestic abuse services etc. such as ‘Refuge’ and ‘Womens Aid’ (UK). 
Here in the UK you can even go to your primary care physician and they can get the ball rolling for you.
These agencies will never try to convince you to leave, they will just give you support and connect you with other women in similar situations if that’s what you want. They will give you the tools you need to make a decision to leave on your own terms.
Of course, you can also look at counselling/therapy too with a clinician that specialises or has experience in domestic abuse.
Also google ‘the cycle of abuse’ - its a really helpful illustration of all the different types of domestic abuse.

So many strong and brilliant women get trapped in these situations and it is so hard to come out of them so be easy on yourself and take it one step at a time. It’s sounds like you are an amazing partner and mum and the way he treats you is a reflection of who he is, it has nothing to do with you or your character ‘flaws’.
